one_liner: Two table-free ARM NEON in-place whitespace strippers, built as alternatives to Lemire's scalar and lookup-table NEON despacers; no published timings.
what_it_does: Removes every byte at or below 0x20 (space, LF, CR, tab, NUL and other control bytes) from a char buffer in place and returns the new length, with the same size_t f(char *bytes, size_t howmany) signature as Lemire's despace(). The repository is an iOS benchmark app: two kernels by Derek Ledbetter (neon_interleaved_despace in interleaved_despacer.c, neon_unzipping_despace in unzipping_despacer.c) sit next to copies of Lemire's scalar despace and AArch64 neontbl_despace in despacer.h. Results appear on the device screen when Run is tapped; none are recorded.
how_it_is_fast: Both kernels de-interleave 64 bytes with vld4q_u8, compare against 0x20 and pack the keep flags into one byte per 8 input bytes, then turn each flag byte into an 8-lane shuffle index vector computed in registers, so the 1 MiB shufmask table that neontbl_despace indexes with a 16-bit movemask is gone. The interleaved kernel finds set bits by repeated lowest-set-bit isolation (x & (x-1) with vcntq_u8 on the trailing ones); the unzipping kernel splits alternating set bits with a carry-less multiply by all ones (vmulq_p8 prefix XOR) applied three times, reading the last two bit positions with vcntq_u8 and vclzq_u8. Each 8-byte group is then gathered with vtbl1_u8 (or vqtbl1q_u8 on AArch64) and stored with an overlapping 8-byte vst1_u8, advancing the output pointer by the popcount.
when_to_use: In-place stripping of whitespace and control bytes from ASCII buffers on ARMv7 NEON or AArch64 (phones, Apple silicon, Graviton-class servers) when a 1 MiB lookup table is unwelcome.
As a reference for table-free NEON stream compaction (bit-isolation or polynomial-multiply index generation) to adapt to other byte filters.
Buffers of at least a few hundred bytes: the vector loops need 128 bytes (interleaved) or 256 bytes (unzipping) before they run; shorter inputs fall to the scalar tail.
Codebases that can take public-domain source drops and will run their own benchmark, since the repository gives no numbers.
when_not_to_use: x86 or any non-NEON target: the functions are not even declared without __ARM_NEON; use lemire/despacer, which also has SSE/AVX variants and published cycle counts.
Non-ASCII (UTF-8) text on Apple platforms or any target where char is signed: the scalar tails delete bytes 0x80-0xFF while the vector body keeps them (see gotchas).
When only space, LF and CR should go: tabs, NUL and all other control bytes are removed too.
Anyone needing measured evidence or maintenance: no timings were ever published and the code has been untouched since 2017-07-20.
Out-of-place use without adaptation: the kernels are written for in-place operation and store 8 bytes at a time past the logical end of the output.

integration.dependencies: none beyond arm_neon.h; the headers include the Apple SDK header <ConditionalMacros.h>, which must be removed to build outside Xcode
integration.min_toolchain: C99 with clang (Xcode 8 era); relies on clang-specific _Pragma("unroll") (GCC ignores it with a warning) and on clang accepting a uint8x16_t initialiser for a poly8x16_t in the unzipping kernel; the benchmark harness folds a const-sized initialised array, a clang extension
integration.platforms: ARMv7 with NEON (vtbl1_u8 path) and AArch64 (vqtbl1q_u8 path in the interleaved kernel); no scalar fallback for other targets
integration.thread_safety: not documented; both kernels touch only the caller's buffer and no shared state, so concurrent calls on separate buffers should be safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signature and in-place contract as despacer's despace(), but NEON-only, and on signed-char targets the tail handles bytes 0x80-0xFF differently from the vector body

gotchas: Signed-char correctness bug, untested by the harness: the vector body keeps bytes 0x80-0xFF (unsigned vcgtq_u8 compare against 32), but the scalar tail of both kernels does 'const char c = *source++; if (c > space)', so on Apple arm64 and other signed-char targets any UTF-8 byte in the last 1-127 (interleaved) or 1-255 (unzipping) bytes is deleted. The scalar baseline despace() in despacer.h also uses signed char and deletes every non-ASCII byte there, while Lemire's neontbl_despace tail uses unsigned char. The benchmark cannot see this because fillwithtext() loops 'while (buffer[i] <= 32)', which rejects every negative char, so the test data on iOS is pure 7-bit ASCII.

Harness timer: gettimeofday with microsecond resolution over a 32 KiB buffer, best of 100 runs, printed under 'ns per operation' though the figure is nanoseconds per input byte; at sub-nanosecond-per-byte speeds one run lasts only tens of microseconds, so each figure carries several percent of quantisation.

The workload has only about 3% whitespace (1% each of space, LF and CR), far below prose; that keeps the baseline neontbl_despace's 1 MiB table mostly on a few hot entries, so the harness does not exercise the table-cache pressure the table-free kernels are designed to avoid.

Every vst1_u8 writes a full 8 bytes and advances by the popcount, so the output region needs 8 bytes of slack; in place this stays inside already-consumed input, but a copying variant must allocate extra room. The 2.87 MB bigtable.h defines a non-const, non-static 1 MiB global in a header, so despacer.h can be included in only one translation unit.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lemire/despacer (Despacer) in nearly every case: it covers x86 and ARM, has published cycle-per-byte results and a maintained repository. Pick space-pruner only when you specifically want a table-free NEON compaction kernel to study or adapt, and test it yourself on non-ASCII input first.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing was measured in public: the repository holds an iOS app that times scalar despace, Lemire's AArch64 neontbl_despace and the two new NEON kernels on a 32 KiB random ASCII buffer with about 3% whitespace, but no results, device, compiler flags or screenshots are committed, and the Lemire blog posts that discuss NEON despacing could not be opened here.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-07-20 after a two-week burst of 35 commits; the README declares the project public domain (no LICENSE file, no patent grant, copyright notices on the Lemire-derived code removed), and the two kernels are small enough to vendor once the Apple header and the signed-char tail are fixed.
